The Buyids, or Buwayhids, were a Shia Iranian dynasty from Daylam, the mountains south of the Caspian, who ruled most of Iran and Iraq from 934 to 1062. See also the Buyid dynasty page. They are shown here in 1000 and, as the map has it, 1200, long after they were gone.

Three brothers, sons of a fisherman named Buya, rose as soldiers and carved out separate emirates. In 945 one of them, Ahmad, entered Baghdad. The Abbasid caliphs kept their title but now lived under Buyid control, giving the Buyid emirs titles such as Mu'izz al-Dawla.

The greatest of them, Adud al-Dawla, ruled from 949 to 983 from Shiraz and Baghdad, built hospitals and dams, and united the family lands for a time. The Buyids backed Twelver Shia rites and patronised Persian and Arabic learning. After him the family split and quarrelled. In 1055 the Seljuk leader Tughril took Baghdad, and the last Buyid emirates fell soon after.
